title: Korean Galbi (Grilled Short Ribs)
finish: Caramelized edges
summary: Flanken-cut short ribs in a sweet-savory soy and Asian pear marinade, grilled hot and fast Korean BBQ-style.
story: Galbi is Korea's backyard barbecue: thin-cut short ribs soaked overnight in soy, sugar, garlic, and grated Asian pear — the pear tenderizes and sweetens at once. Then screaming-hot grill, a few minutes a side, wrapped in lettuce with ssamjang and kimchi. Fast, loud, and gone in minutes.

items: 4 lbs beef short ribs, flanken cut 1/2-inch thick

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade, pour over the ribs, and refrigerate overnight — 8 hours minimum.

steps.title: Grill hot
steps.body: Grill over screaming-hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side until caramelized at the edges.

steps.title: Wrap and eat
steps.body: Serve with lettuce, ssamjang, kimchi, and rice. Wrap a bite of everything and eat it in one go — that's the way.

title: Filipino Pork BBQ Skewers
finish: Charred edges, 145°F+
summary: The Philippines' street-corner classic: pork in a sweet banana-ketchup marinade, skewered and grilled over hot coals.
story: Walk past any grill in the Philippines and you'll smell these — pork shoulder soaked overnight in banana ketchup, soy, calamansi, and brown sugar, then grilled fast over screaming coals until the edges char and caramelize. Sweet, sticky, smoky. Make extra; they disappear.

items: 3 lbs pork shoulder, sliced thin (about 1/4 inch)

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade and pour over the pork. Refrigerate overnight — 8 hours minimum for the full sweet-savory soak.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Thread the pork onto bamboo skewers (soaked 30 minutes so they don't burn), weaving the slices accordion-style.

steps.title: Grill hot
steps.body: Grill over hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side, basting with the reserved marinade, until charred at the edges and cooked through.

title: Yakitori (Chicken & Negi Skewers)
finish: 165°F, lacquered with tare
summary: Japan's charcoal-grilled chicken skewers — thigh and negi onion, brushed with sweet-savory tare over blazing coals.
story: Yakitori is Japanese barbecue stripped to the essentials: chicken thigh, long green onion, blazing binchotan charcoal, and tare — a syrupy glaze of soy, mirin, sake, and sugar. The trick is brushing the tare on again and again until the skewers shine like lacquer. Salt-and-pepper (shio) is the purist's move; tare is the crowd-pleaser.

items: 2 lbs boneless skin-on chicken thighs, cut in 1-inch cubes
4 stalks negi (long green onion), cut in 1 1/2-inch pieces

steps.title: Make the tare
steps.body: Simmer the tare ingredients 10 minutes until slightly syrupy. Set aside — this is liquid gold.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Alternate chicken and negi on the skewers, packing them snug.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over the hottest charcoal you've got, turning often and brushing with tare every turn, 8-10 minutes until the chicken hits 165°F and shines.

title: Russian Shashlik
finish: Juicy, 145°F+
summary: Russia's iconic pork-neck kebab: onion and vinegar marinade, skewered tight, grilled over gray coals.
story: Shashlik is Russia's answer to barbecue — pork neck (the fattiest, juiciest cut) drowned in sliced onion, vinegar, salt, and pepper, then grilled over coals burned down to gray ash. The Soviet-era classic uses nothing fancier than that, and it's perfect. Serve it with pickled onions and don't you dare use a fork.

items: 4 lbs pork neck, cut in 2-inch cubes
3 large onions, sliced in thick rings

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Squeeze half the onion rings with your hands to release the juice, then mix everything with the pork. Dissolve the vinegar in the water and pour over. Refrigerate 6 hours to overnight — longer is better.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Thread the pork tightly onto flat metal skewers, alternating with onion rings. Tight packing keeps the meat juicy.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over coals burned to gray-white ash — no open flame. Turn frequently, 15-20 minutes, sprinkling with water if flames flare. Cut one open to check; serve on the skewer with pickled onions.

title: German Schwenkbraten
finish: 145°F internal
summary: Saarland's swinging-grate pork steaks — mustard, onion, and juniper marinade over beechwood fire.
story: Yes, the Germans barbecue — and in Saarland they take it seriously. Thick pork neck steaks marinate a full day in mustard, onion, juniper, and paprika, then grill on a swinging grate (the Schwenker) over beechwood embers. Serve it with potato salad, a crusty roll, and a cold beer, the way it's done.

items: 4 pork neck steaks, about 8 oz each, 1 1/2 inches thick

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Rub the pork with the mustard, then mix with all marinade ingredients. Refrigerate 24-48 hours — the long soak is what makes it Schwenkbraten.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Shake off the excess marinade. Grill over medium beechwood or charcoal embers about 10 minutes per side to 145°F internal, grilling the onion slices alongside.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 5 minutes. Serve with potato salad, crusty rolls, and beer.

title: Chicken Satay with Peanut Sauce
finish: 165°F, lightly charred
summary: Thai-style turmeric chicken skewers over hot coals, with a rich coconut-peanut dipping sauce.
story: Satay is Southeast Asia's great street food — chicken strips in a turmeric-coconut marinade, grilled fast over charcoal, dunked in peanut sauce. The marinade does double duty: color, flavor, and just enough sugar to char at the edges. Don't skimp on the peanut sauce; it's half the dish.

items: 2 lbs chicken thigh, cut in long strips

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Coat the chicken in the marinade and refrigerate at least 2 hours, up to overnight. Thread onto skewers.

steps.title: Make the sauce
steps.body: Simmer the peanut sauce ingredients 5 minutes, whisking, until smooth and glossy. Thin with a splash of water if needed.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side until lightly charred and 165°F inside. Serve with the warm peanut sauce, cucumber, and red onion.

title: Tacos al Pastor
finish: Crisped edges, charred pineapple
summary: Achiote-marinated pork stacked trompo-style with pineapple on top — the taco that Lebanese immigrants gave Mexico.
story: Al pastor is shawarma's Mexican grandchild: Lebanese immigrants brought the vertical spit, Mexico gave it achiote, dried chiles, and pineapple. At home, stack the marinated pork on a vertical skewer (or just grill it hot in batches) with a pineapple on top, shave it thin, and build tacos with charred pineapple, onion, and cilantro.

items: 4 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed, seeded, and soaked

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Blend the adobo ingredients smooth and coat the pork. Refrigerate overnight — the achiote needs time to work.

steps.title: Stack
steps.body: Stack the pork on a vertical skewer set in a halved onion base, crowned with the pineapple (trompo-style). No vertical setup? Just grill the slices hot in batches.

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Roast or grill, turning, until the edges crisp and char — about 45-60 minutes on a trompo, less in batches. Shave thin.

steps.title: Build tacos
steps.body: Pile onto warm corn tortillas with charred pineapple chunks, onion, cilantro, and lime.

title: Hawaiian Huli Huli Chicken
finish: 165°F internal, caramelized
summary: Hawaii's roadside legend: chicken in a soy-pineapple-ginger glaze, turned again and again over the fire.
story: Huli huli means 'turn turn' — and that's the whole technique. Since 1955, when Ernest Morgado grilled it for a farmers' gathering, this soy-pineapple-ginger chicken has been Hawaii's fundraiser and roadside staple. Marinate it, grill it, and keep turning and basting until the glaze caramelizes dark and sticky. Grill some pineapple rings alongside — that's not optional.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade ingredients. Reserve 1 cup for basting; pour the rest over the chicken and refrigerate 4 hours or overnight.

steps.title: Grill and turn
steps.body: Grill over medium heat, turning every 5 minutes and basting with the reserved marinade — huli huli, turn turn — about 35-45 minutes.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Cook to 165°F internal with a dark caramelized glaze. Rest 10 minutes. Serve with grilled pineapple and rice.

title: Israeli Shishlik
finish: 165°F internal, charred edges
summary: Israel's backyard skewers: cumin-and-paprika chicken grilled over coals, served with hummus and Israeli salad.
story: In Israel, barbecue is 'al ha'esh' — on the fire — and shishlik is the weeknight hero: chicken cubes in olive oil, lemon, cumin, and paprika, grilled fast over hot coals. No fancy equipment, no long smoke, just bold spice and fire. Pile it into pita with hummus, Israeli salad, and a squeeze of lemon, and dinner's done.

items: 2 1/2 lbs boneless chicken thighs, cut in 1 1/2-inch cubes
Israeli salad (diced tomato, cucumber, red onion, parsley, lemon)

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Toss the chicken cubes in all the marinade ingredients. Refrigerate at least 1 hour, up to 8.

steps.title: Skewer and grill
steps.body: Thread onto skewers. Grill hot, 3-4 minutes per side, until charred at the edges and 165°F internal.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Slide into warm pita with hummus, Israeli salad, and lemon. Eat over the plate — it drips.

title: South African Boerewors
finish: 160°F internal
summary: The coil sausage of the South African braai: coriander-scented beef and pork, grilled in one long spiral.
story: Boerewors — 'farmer's sausage' — is the heart of the South African braai. By law it's mostly meat, but the soul is in the spice: toasted coriander above all, with nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper behind it. It's made and grilled in one long coil, never links. If you've got a grinder and stuffer, make it from scratch; if not, find a South African butcher and grill it right — medium coals, turned gently, never pierced.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Chill the meat and fat until nearly frozen. Grind through a coarse plate into a cold bowl.

steps.title: Season and mix
steps.body: Add the vinegar and spices. Mix with cold hands just until tacky — don't overwork it. Fry a small patty and adjust salt.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings in one continuous coil — no links. Prick any air pockets.

steps.title: Braai
steps.body: Grill over medium coals 20-25 minutes, turning gently, to 160°F internal. Never pierce the casing. Slice the coil at the table.

title: Ember Southwest Rub
finish: Mixed and jarred
summary: Chipotle, cumin, and Hatch chile — the dry half of the Ember Southwest lineup.
story: Every sauce needs its rub. This is the dry half of the Southwest lineup: chipotle for smoke, cumin for earth, Hatch chile powder for that New Mexico kick Kelly loves, and brown sugar to caramelize it all. Rub it on the Hatch thighs, dust it over wings, or shake it on ribs — then finish with the Ember Southwest BBQ Sauce.

items: 1 Tbsp Hatch green chile powder (or New Mexico chile powder)

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk everything together, breaking up any lumps in the brown sugar.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Keep in an airtight jar away from heat and light. Good for 6 months.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Rub generously on chicken, pork, or beef 1 hour before cooking (overnight for big cuts). Pair with Ember Southwest BBQ Sauce.

title: Smoked Barbecue Chicken
finish: Thighs 175°F, breast 160°F
summary: A whole bird spatchcocked and halved, rubbed with Ember rub and finished with a sticky Ember sauce glaze. The backyard bird done right.
story: Halves are the working man's chicken — cheaper than breasts, more forgiving than a whole bird, and every piece gets smoke and sauce. Take a whole chicken, spatchcock it, and cut it in half. Season with Ember rub, smoke it steady, and don't sauce too early or the sugar burns before the meat's done. This is Kelly's backyard bird, the one from the grill photo.

items: Ember rub (or your favorite rub), enough to coat
1 cup Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce), thinned with a splash of apple juice if it's thick

steps.title: Spatchcock and halve
steps.body: Cut out the backbone, press the breast flat, then cut the bird in half through the breastbone. Pat dry. Season all over with Ember rub — under the skin where you can reach.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 275–300°F with hickory or apple, skin-side up. About 2 to 2½ hours.

steps.title: Glaze — your call
steps.body: When the thighs read 165°F, it’s your choice: brush on the Ember sauce and give it 20–30 more minutes so the glaze sets and gets sticky, or leave the bird dry if you like the bark just the way it is.

steps.title: Rest and serve
steps.body: Pull at 175°F in the thigh (breast 160°F). Rest 10 minutes, then cut each half into leg and breast portions.

proTips.text: Sauce late — if you sauce at all. Sugar burns, so the glaze goes on in the last half hour, not the first. No sauce? The bark stands on its own.
Halves over direct heat for the last 5 minutes if you want the skin to bite through.

milestones.label: On the pit
milestones.hint: 275–300°F, skin up, hickory or apple.

milestones.label: Glaze
milestones.hint: Thighs 165°F — brush on Ember sauce.

milestones.label: Pull
milestones.hint: Thighs 175°F, breast 160°F. Rest 10 minutes.

title: Smoked Canadian Bacon
summary: Turn a pork loin into deli-style Canadian bacon with a simple 7-day cure and a kiss of smoke.
story: Canadian bacon isn't bacon at all — it's cured pork loin, smoked gentle and sliced thin. The cure does the real work over a week in the fridge; the smoker just finishes the job. Slice it thin for breakfast sandwiches, chop it into hash, or eat it cold right off the slicer.

items: 1 whole pork loin, 3–4 lbs, trimmed of excess fat and silverskin

steps.title: Mix the cure
steps.body: Stir the kosher salt, brown sugar, pink curing salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and onion powder together in a bowl.

steps.title: Rub the loin
steps.body: Coat the pork loin all over with the cure — every surface, no bare spots.

steps.title: Cure 7 days
steps.body: Seal the loin in a large zip-top or vacuum bag, squeezing out the air. Set it on a tray in the fridge and flip the bag once a day for 7 days. It will release liquid — that's normal.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Rinse the loin under cold water and pat dry. Set it on a rack over a tray, uncovered, in the fridge overnight. The dry surface takes smoke better.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Run the smoker at 200–225°F with fruit wood or hickory. Smoke the loin to 145°F internal, about 2 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Rest, chill, slice
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes, then chill fully in the fridge before slicing thin, like deli meat.

proTips.text: Don't skip the pink curing salt — it's what keeps the meat rosy and safe through the long cure. 1 teaspoon per 5 lbs of meat is the rule.
Chill it firm before slicing — a cold loin cuts thin and even. Fry slices for breakfast sandwiches or chop into hash.

title: Kelly's Smoked Baby Back Ribs
summary: Real ribs off Kelly's smoker — sweet heat, crackly crust, clean bite off the bone.
story: Baby backs are the leaner, quicker rib — they take smoke beautifully and don't need all day. The crust is the thing: a little turbinado sugar over the rub goes crackly under the heat, and the sauce goes on late so it sets instead of burns.

items: Ember rub (or your favorite rib rub), enough to coat
Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce), for glazing
Butter, brown sugar, honey, and a sprinkle of rub (for wrapping, optional)

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Pull the membrane from the bone side. Coat the racks all over with Ember rub, then a light shake of turbinado sugar over the top.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with hickory or oak, bone-side down, about 3 hours — until the bark sets and the color goes deep.

steps.title: Wrap or ride it out
steps.body: Your choice: wrap in foil with pats of butter, a handful of brown sugar, a drizzle of honey, a sprinkle of extra rub, and a splash of cherry Dr Pepper or whatever flavor soda you like for about an hour for bend-tender ribs, or skip the wrap and ride it out for a firmer bite.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush on the Ember sauce and give it 20–30 minutes so the glaze sets sticky.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, then slice between the bones.

proTips.text: Turbinado for the crust — crackly, not burnt.
Sauce late. Sugar burns — the glaze goes on at the end.
Cherry Dr Pepper mixed with brown sugar, mopped or sprayed on during the cook, builds a crackling bark.

title: Smoked Pork Tenderloin
summary: Smoke it gentle, then char it like a steakhouse steak — juicy, barely pink, crosshatch crust.
story: There's a hundred ways to do a tenderloin, but treat it like a good steak and it eats like one. Smoke brings the flavor; a screaming-hot finish on GrillGrates brings the crust. Pull it at 155°F and it stays juicy with just a blush of pink.

items: 1–2 pork tenderloins, about 1 lb each, silverskin trimmed
Ember rub (or your favorite steak seasoning), enough to coat
Light coat of olive oil or yellow mustard as a binder

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Trim the silverskin. Rub with a light coat of oil or mustard, then season all over with Ember rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Smoke to about 140°F internal — roughly an hour.

steps.title: Char it
steps.body: Move to screaming-hot GrillGrates over direct heat. Roll the tenderloins to char all sides with crosshatch marks, pulling at 155°F internal.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, then slice into medallions. Barely pink, juicy, steakhouse crust.

proTips.text: I run mine to 155°F — stays juicy with just a blush of pink. Don't let it ride past that.
GrillGrates are worth it — that crosshatch char eats like a professional steakhouse.

title: Smoked Pork Chops
summary: Thick-cut chops with a kiss of smoke, finished like a steak — crosshatch char and a sticky Ember glaze.
story: A thick pork chop wants the same treatment as a good steak. Start it low so it takes on a little smoke, then move it over direct heat on the GrillGrates and char it with crosshatch marks. Brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze at the end, pull it at 155°F, and it stays juicy. No wrapping — a chop this thick doesn't need it.

items: Mayonnaise or yellow mustard, a thin coat as a binder
Ember rub (or your favorite pork rub), enough to coat
½ cup Ember Finishing Glaze (or your favorite barbecue sauce)

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Pat the chops dry. Smear on a thin coat of mayonnaise or mustard as a binder, then season all over with Ember rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Smoke the chops to about 135°F internal — roughly 45 minutes to an hour, depending on thickness.

steps.title: Char and glaze
steps.body: Move the chops to screaming-hot GrillGrates over direct heat. Sear with crosshatch marks, turning once, and brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze in the last minute or two. Pull at 155°F internal.

steps.title: Rest and serve
steps.body: Rest 5–10 minutes so the juices settle, then serve. Juicy and smoky, with a steakhouse char.

proTips.text: I never wrap my pork chops. A thick chop doesn't need it — the smoke and the char do all the work.
Treat the finish like a steak: hot grates, crosshatch marks, and don't let it ride past 155°F or it'll dry out.

title: Smoked Barbecue Meatballs
summary: Beef-and-pork meatballs smoked low, then glazed with Ember sauce and cherry preserves — sweet, a little tart, sticky.
story: Everybody knows the grape-jelly potluck meatball. This is the pit version: real smoke first, then a cherry glaze. Cherry belongs with beef and pork — it's the same fruit behind the cherry Dr Pepper bark trick — and it makes these yours instead of a copy of everybody else's.

items: 2 Tbsp Ember rub (or your favorite rub), plus a little extra for dusting
1 cup Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce)
½ tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix everything gentle, just until it comes together. Overworking the mix is what makes meatballs eat like hockey pucks.

steps.title: Roll and chill
steps.body: Roll into balls about 1½ inches across — wet hands keep the mix from sticking to you. You should get about 24. Rest them in the fridge 20–30 minutes so they hold their shape on the pit.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Dust the tops with a little more rub and smoke about an hour, until they hit 160°F inside.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Warm the Ember sauce and cherry preserves together until the preserves melt in — stir in the red pepper flakes if you're using them. Brush the glaze over the meatballs and give them 10–15 more minutes so it sets sticky.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve them as a pick-up appetizer with toothpicks, or pile them up as a main.

proTips.text: You can put red pepper flakes in it if you want to make them spicier.
Don't overmix — gentle hands keep them tender.

title: Porcupine Meatballs and Tomato Gravy
summary: Kelly and Kristy's — big beef-and-rice meatballs simmered the whole time in tomato juice until the rice pokes out like quills, finished with a roux-thickened tomato gravy. On the stove, or with a little light smoke on the pit.
story: Kelly's mama made these when he was a kid — one of the things he liked that she cooked — and now he and Kristy make them. The meatballs braise in a big can of tomato juice from start to finish, and the gravy is that same juice at the end, thickened with a roux until it coats a spoon. It is a family batch and it is served the family way: over mashed potatoes, with plenty of gravy spooned over.

items: 1 to 1½ cups uncooked long-grain white rice
1 jalapeño, diced fine (optional — if you want them spicy)
1 can (14–15 oz) whole or diced tomatoes (optional — up to the cook)

steps.title: Mix and roll big
steps.body: Mix all the meatball ingredients and roll them big, about 3 inches across — 8 to 12 meatballs. One pound ain't nothing; this is a family batch.

steps.title: Into the juice
steps.body: Set the meatballs in a Dutch oven or deep pot and pour the whole big can of tomato juice over them. They cook in the juice the whole time. If you want whole or diced tomatoes in yours, add them to the juice now — it's up to the cook.

steps.title: On the stove
steps.body: Cover and simmer low about 1 hour, until the rice is tender and poking out of the meatballs like quills.

steps.title: Or on the smoker
steps.body: Dutch oven on the pit at 250°F with a light wood like apple or cherry. Lid off or cracked the first hour so they take a little smoke, then cover and cook 1½–2 hours total, until the rice is tender.

steps.title: Make the gravy
steps.body: Work the butter and flour together into a roux and stir it into the juice around the meatballs. Simmer a few more minutes until it thickens into a tomato gravy.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Over mashed potatoes, with plenty of gravy spooned over.

proTips: "If you want to get spicy, you can add jalapeños." — Kelly
Whole or diced tomatoes in the juice are the cook's call — "It's all up to the cook." — Kelly
Light wood on the smoker version — heavy smoke would overpower the tomato gravy.
The rice goes in uncooked. It cooks in the juice, and that is what makes the quills.

title: Hawaiian Shish Kebabs
summary: Kelly's Hawaiian skewers — chicken and pork in a soy-pineapple marinade, threaded with big pineapple chunks, bell pepper, and onion, grilled until the edges char.
story: These are Kelly's own, off his grill. The pineapple goes right on the skewer with the meat, and the marinade is the Hawaiian way — soy, pineapple juice, and brown sugar — so the edges caramelize and catch a little char over the fire. Sweet, salty, smoky, and gone fast.

items: 1½ lbs chicken (thighs or breast), cut in big chunks
1½ lbs pork, cut in big chunks
1 fresh pineapple, cut in big chunks
1 orange bell pepper, cut in squares

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Stir the marinade together, toss the chicken and pork in it, and let it sit at least an hour — a few hours is better.

steps.title: Thread the skewers
steps.body: Meat, pineapple, pepper, onion, repeat. Don't pack them tight or they won't char right.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Over medium-high heat, turning every few minutes, about 12–15 minutes, until the meat is cooked through and the pineapple and peppers have charred edges.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Over rice, straight off the skewers.

proTips: The pineapple isn't decoration — its sugar is what chars and caramelizes the edges.
If you're using wooden skewers, soak them in water first so they don't burn up on you.
Leave a little space between pieces on the skewer — crowded meat steams instead of grilling.

title: Over-the-Top Smoked Chili
summary: The chili everybody's cooking right now — a seasoned beef loaf smokes on the grate over a Dutch oven of chili, dripping into the pot the whole cook, then gets crumbled in to finish.
story: Over-the-top chili is the one all over the BBQ sites this year, and the trick earns it: the meat never touches the chili until it is smoked, so the pot catches two hours of seasoned drippings while the loaf takes on smoke and a crust. Crumble it in, let it simmer, and you get a chili with smoke all the way through instead of just on top.

items: 2 Tbsp Ember rub (or your favorite beef rub)

steps.title: Form the loaf
steps.body: Mix the beef with the rub, chili powder, and cumin and form it into one tight loaf. Tight matters — a loose loaf will sag and break up on the grate.

steps.title: Build the pot
steps.body: Everything for the pot goes in a Dutch oven, stirred together.

steps.title: Set up the pit
steps.body: Pit at 250–275°F, hickory or oak. The Dutch oven sits on the lower grate and the loaf goes on the grate right over the pot, so every drip lands in the chili.

steps.title: Smoke the loaf
steps.body: About 2 hours, until the loaf hits 150°F inside and has a good crust.

steps.title: Crumble and simmer
steps.body: Crumble the loaf into the pot, stir it through, and simmer 1–2 more hours with the lid cracked, until it is as thick as you like it.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Cheese, sour cream, and saltines or oyster crackers. Kelly's jalapeño cheddar cornbread sits perfect next to it.

proTips: The loaf is the smoke catcher — the pot below is mostly steaming, so the meat is where the smoke flavor comes from. Do not rush the two hours.
If your pit only has one grate, set the pot on the grate and lay a small cooling rack across the top of the pot for the loaf. Same trick.
Like every chili, it is better the second day.

title: Classic Apple Cider Spritz
summary: The old reliable — apple juice and apple cider vinegar in a spray bottle. Keeps pork moist, helps the bark set, and the vinegar cuts the fat just enough.
story: If a pitmaster owns one spray bottle, this is what's in it. Two ingredients every kitchen already has, and it works on just about anything pork — butts, ribs, loins. The apple brings a little sweetness, the vinegar keeps it honest.

steps.title: Stir it up
steps.body: Apple juice and vinegar in a measuring cup. If you use the brown sugar, stir till it melts in — it adds a little bark-building sweetness.

steps.title: Into the bottle
steps.body: Pour it into a clean food-grade spray bottle and give it a shake.

steps.title: Spritz the cook
steps.body: Wait till the bark has started to set — about 90 minutes in — then spritz every 45–60 minutes. Lid up, quick spray, lid back down. No drowning it.

proTips: Never spritz before the rub sets — you will wash it right off. The bark should look dry and set before the first spray.
Shake the bottle before every round; the sugar settles.
Leftovers keep a week in the fridge. Rinse the sprayer head so it doesn't clog.

title: Ember Cherry Dr Pepper Spritz
summary: Kelly's signature — cherry Dr Pepper with brown sugar melted in. This is the spritz behind the crackling bark on his ribs, chicken, pork butt, and pork belly.
story: This one's Kelly's own. The cherry soda brings the fruit, the brown sugar caramelizes as it hits the heat, and together they build a crust that crackles when you slice it. It's the bottle that lives next to his pit.

steps.title: Warm and melt
steps.body: Soda and brown sugar in a small pot over low heat, stirred till the sugar is melted clean through. Don't boil it.

steps.title: Cool and bottle
steps.body: Let it cool, then into a clean spray bottle.

steps.title: Spritz for the crackle
steps.body: Once the bark has set, spritz every 45–60 minutes. Ribs, chicken, pork butt, pork belly — this is the one that makes the crust crackle.

proTips: The sugar is what crackles — don't leave it out and don't swap in diet soda.
Flat soda works fine; the bubbles don't matter, the sugar does.
A splash of this same mix goes in Kelly's rib wrap, too.

title: Cola Brown Sugar Spritz
summary: The Dr Pepper's first cousin — cola and brown sugar with a splash of vinegar to keep it from going candy-sweet. Same crackle, different soda.
story: Not everybody keeps cherry Dr Pepper in the house, but most folks have a cola. This one drinks from the same well — soda sugar for the crust, brown sugar for depth, and one spoon of vinegar so it tastes like barbecue and not dessert.

steps.title: Warm and melt
steps.body: Cola and brown sugar over low heat till the sugar melts, then stir in the vinegar.

steps.title: Cool and bottle
steps.body: Cool it down and into a clean spray bottle.

steps.title: Spritz the cook
steps.body: After the bark sets, every 45–60 minutes — ribs and pork take to it best.

proTips: The vinegar spoon is small but it matters — skip it and the spritz goes flat-sweet.
Real sugar cola only; diet won't caramelize.

title: Sweet Tea Peach Spritz
summary: Sweet tea and peach nectar — a gentle, Southern spritz that loves pork and chicken and never fights the rub.
story: Some cooks want the spritz to whisper instead of shout. Sweet tea brings a mellow tannin, peach brings the fruit, and together they keep pork and chicken moist with a flavor that stays in the background where a light spritz belongs.

items: 1/2 cup peach nectar (or the juice from canned peaches)

steps.title: Stir it up
steps.body: Tea and peach nectar together in a measuring cup. The spoon of vinegar is optional — it just wakes it up.

steps.title: Into the bottle
steps.body: Into a clean spray bottle, no cooking needed.

steps.title: Spritz the cook
steps.body: Once the bark or skin has set, spritz every 45–60 minutes. Pork loin, ribs, and chicken are its best friends.

proTips: No peach nectar in the pantry? The syrup off a can of peaches does the same job.
This one's gentle — it's the spritz for cooks who don't want the soda sweetness.

title: Brisket Spritz
summary: Beef broth, cider vinegar, and Worcestershire — a savory spritz with no sugar in it, so a brisket's bark stays dark and beefy.
story: Brisket doesn't want sweet — it wants beef on beef. This is the Texas way of spritzing: broth for depth, vinegar for a little bite, Worcestershire for the dark savory note. It keeps the bark moist without ever turning it candy.

steps.title: Stir it up
steps.body: Broth, vinegar, and Worcestershire in a measuring cup. No heat, no sugar, nothing to melt.

steps.title: Into the bottle
steps.body: Into a clean spray bottle.

steps.title: Spritz the cook
steps.body: Wait for the bark to set dark — a few hours in — then spritz every 45–60 minutes, mostly the edges and the flat, where brisket dries first.

proTips: Hit the edges and the thin end of the flat hardest — that's where brisket gives up its moisture.
No sugar means no crackle and no candy — that's the point. This bottle is about bark staying dark.

title: Butter & Herb Smoked Cornish Hens
summary: Little hens with herb butter worked under the skin — thyme, rosemary, and basil — smoked over cherry until the skin browns deep and the butter bastes them from the inside.
story: A Cornish hen is a one-person chicken, and that is the whole charm — everybody at the table gets their own bird. Kelly does his the butter-and-herb way: a stick of butter loaded with Ember Herb Rub, half of it under the skin where it bastes the meat, half over the top where it browns it. The herb trio — thyme, rosemary, and dried basil — is the Malcolm Reed way, and the rub is Kelly's own.

items: 1 tsp Ember Herb Rub, for a light dusting (optional)

steps.title: Brine (optional)
steps.body: Stir the salt and sugar into the water till melted and sink the hens in for about 4 hours in the fridge. It seasons the meat itself — worth it if you've got the time, fine to skip if you don't.

steps.title: Make the butter
steps.body: Mash the Ember Herb Rub and garlic into the soft butter till it's one spread. That's a tablespoon of rub per bird — on a small bird, that's the right hand.

steps.title: Butter the birds
steps.body: Pat the hens dry. Loosen the skin over the breast with your fingers and push half the butter up under it, spreading toward the thighs. Rub the rest all over the outside, and dust lightly with extra rub if you like.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250–275°F over cherry or apple wood, skin up, about 45–60 minutes. The butter bastes them from the inside while they take the smoke.

steps.title: Crisp and finish
steps.body: Kick the heat up at the end — or a quick pass over direct heat — to brown the skin deep, to 165°F in the thigh. Spoon the buttery drippings from the pan over the birds.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Ten minutes. One hen per person, butter and herbs in every bite.

proTips: Little birds cook fast — this is not a wander-off cook.
Want them faster? Spatchcock each hen flat — same butter, same herbs, about 10 minutes less.
The butter mix is the Ember Herb Rub at work — keep a jar of the rub and this whole recipe gets easy.

title: Ember Herb Rub
summary: Thyme, rosemary, and dried basil over a salt-and-garlic base — the herb rub behind the Butter & Herb Cornish Hens, and good anywhere a bird or a pork loin needs green flavor.
story: Kelly needed an herb rub of his own, so this one got built on the trio Malcolm Reed cooks with — thyme, rosemary, and dried basil — over a plain salt, garlic, and pepper base with nothing sweet and nothing red in it. It's a green rub, and it earns its keep two ways: straight on the meat, or mashed into butter.

steps.title: Crush the rosemary
steps.body: Rosemary is pushy and poky — crush it fine with your fingers, a mortar, or a quick pulse in a spice grinder, so it blends instead of stabbing.

steps.title: Stir it together
steps.body: Everything in a bowl, stirred till it's even — green all through the salt.

steps.title: Jar it
steps.body: Into a sealed jar in the pantry. Dried herbs keep their punch for months.

proTips: The famous use: 1 stick of soft butter + 2 Tbsp of this rub = the herb butter for two Cornish hens — a tablespoon a bird.
Table salt runs saltier than kosher by the spoon — if that's what you've got, use a shade less.
Try it on chicken, turkey, pork loin and chops, and roasted potatoes.

title: Kelly's Smoked Carnitas
summary: Pork butt smoked till the bark sets, braised down in citrus, garlic, and cumin till it falls apart, then crisped so the edges catch — carnitas that still eats like barbecue.
story: Carnitas is pork shoulder taken past pulled — cooked down in citrus and its own juices till it falls apart, then crisped so the edges catch and brown. Kelly's way starts it on the smoker first, so the smoke is in the meat before the braise ever starts. This is the last of the four pork cooks he picked out for the app, and it might be the best of the bunch.

items: 2–3 Tbsp Ember pork rub (or your favorite pork rub)
1 cup Mexican lager or chicken broth

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Score the fat cap, rub the butt heavy all over, and let it rest an hour on the counter — or overnight in the fridge if you're thinking ahead.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F over hickory or oak, 5–6 hours, till the bark is set deep and it probes around 165°F.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Set the butt in a pan with the orange and lime juice, onion, garlic, cumin, oregano, and the lager or broth. Cover tight and back on at 300°F till it probes like butter, 200–205°F — another 1 1/2 to 2 hours, give or take.

steps.title: Shred
steps.body: Pull the meat apart into chunks and shreds. Ditch the bone and the big pieces of fat. Keep the braising juices — that's liquid gold.

steps.title: Crisp
steps.body: Spread the meat out with a ladle of the braising juices over it and crisp the edges — under a hot broiler, on a flat top, or back on the smoker running hot — till the corners catch and brown. Serve on warm tortillas with onion and cilantro.

proTips: Don't skip the crisp — tender carnitas is good, but the crispy edges are the whole point.
Leftover braising juice goes in the fridge; a spoonful wakes the meat right back up when you reheat it.
Leftovers re-crisp in a hot skillet better than almost any barbecue there is.

title: Esquites (Street Corn in a Cup)
summary: Mexican street corn off the cob and into a cup — smoked corn cut from the cob, stirred warm with mayo, crema, and lime, and heaped up with cotija and Tajín.
story: Elote is the corn on the cob; esquites is the same street corn cut off and served in a cup with a spoon — easier to eat, easier to pass around a crowd. Kelly's version starts the corn on the smoker in its husks, so the kernels pick up real smoke before the char, then everything gets stirred together warm so the sauce coats every bite.

items: 1/4 cup Mexican crema or sour cream
Hot sauce, for whoever wants it (optional)

steps.title: Smoke the corn
steps.body: Husks on, straight on the grate at 225°F over apple or hickory, about 45 minutes. The husk keeps the corn moist while it takes on gentle smoke.

steps.title: Char and cut
steps.body: Pull the husks back and give the ears a quick pass over direct heat till the kernels spot and char here and there. Stand each ear up and cut the kernels off into a big bowl.

steps.title: Warm it through
steps.body: Melt the butter in a skillet, add the kernels, and stir a few minutes till everything is steaming hot.

steps.title: Stir in the mix
steps.body: Off the heat, stir in the mayonnaise, crema, lime juice and zest, garlic, and salt till every kernel is coated.

steps.title: Serve in cups
steps.body: Spoon into cups heaped up, shower with cotija, dust with Tajín, scatter cilantro, and set a lime wedge on each. Hot sauce at the table for whoever wants the heat.

proTips: Cutting the kernels into a bowl set inside a bigger bowl keeps them from jumping all over the counter.
Frozen corn works in a pinch — thaw it and get it dry, then char it hard in the skillet for the spots.
This is the side that disappears first at a cookout. Make more than you think you need.

title: Smoked Prime Rib
summary: A bone-in rib roast dry-brined overnight, rubbed with Ember Herb Rub and coarse pepper, smoked low over oak, rested, and reverse-seared to a deep crust — rosy red edge to edge.
story: Prime rib is the Christmas roast, the special-occasion roast — the one most folks cook once a year and think about the rest of it. It does not need much: a dry brine for the crust, Kelly's Ember Herb Rub with extra coarse pepper (rosemary and thyme were born for this meat), low oak smoke, and a hot finish. Cook it to temperature, slice it thick, and let the table go quiet.

items: Kosher salt, for the dry brine (about 1 tsp per pound)

steps.title: Dry brine
steps.body: Salt the roast all over and set it uncovered in the fridge overnight. The salt seasons it deep and dries the surface — that's what makes the crust.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Pat the roast dry. Work the Ember Herb Rub and the extra coarse pepper into every side. Let it sit out about an hour to take the chill off.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225–250°F over oak or hickory, fat side up. Figure 35–40 minutes a pound, but cook to temperature, not the clock — pull it at 120–125°F in the center for medium-rare.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Tent it loose with foil and rest 30 minutes. The temperature will climb a few degrees while it sits, and the juices settle back in.

steps.title: Reverse sear
steps.body: Into a ripping hot oven at 500°F — or over direct coals — 5–10 minutes, till the outside is crusted deep brown. Watch it close; it goes fast.

steps.title: Slice and serve
steps.body: Carve thick slices, 130–135°F and rosy edge to edge. Warm the drippings with the beef broth for au jus, stir the horseradish cream together cold, and pass both at the table.

proTips: A leave-in thermometer is not optional on a roast this pricey — guesswork is expensive.
Leftover prime rib makes the finest sandwich there is: shaved thin, warm au jus, horseradish cream, crusty roll.
Save the bones. They make a beef broth worth writing home about.

title: Smoked Rabbit in Gravy
summary: Rabbit pieces brined, smoked over hickory for flavor, then braised tender in a Dutch oven and finished in their own gravy — the country way, over mashed potatoes or biscuits.
story: Rabbit is lean as a fence rail, and if you treat it like chicken it will go tough on you. The country answer is the one Kelly cooks by: smoke it first for the flavor, then braise it tender in a pot and let the gravy finish the job. Same road works for squirrel — Kelly will tell you that himself.

items: 1 Tbsp Ember rub (or salt, pepper, garlic, and a little paprika)

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Stir the salt and sugar into the water, sink the rabbit pieces in, and refrigerate 4 hours or overnight. Rabbit wants the brine worse than almost anything — it is that lean.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the pieces dry and season all over with the rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225–250°F over hickory or apple, about an hour. You are not cooking it done here — you are putting the smoke in it.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Into a Dutch oven with the broth, onion, and garlic. Lid on, at 300°F — in the oven or back on the smoker — for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, till the meat is tender and starting to give.

steps.title: Make the gravy
steps.body: Lift the rabbit out and keep it warm. Melt the butter in the pot, whisk in the flour, and cook a minute. Pour the braising liquid back in, whisking, and simmer till it coats a spoon.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rabbit back into the gravy for a minute to warm through. Over mashed potatoes or biscuits — there is no wrong answer.

proTips: Young rabbits are the tender ones; an old, big rabbit just needs more time in the braise, not more heat.
This exact treatment — brine, smoke, braise, gravy — is the squirrel recipe too. Kelly's words.
Do not skip the brine on lean game. It is the difference between tender and shoe leather.

title: Cherry Dr Pepper Turkey
summary: Kelly's signature cherry Dr Pepper and brown sugar — the same crackle he puts on ribs — moved to the Thanksgiving bird: brined, injected with chicken-broth butter, spritzed, and glazed deep red mahogany.
story: Everybody else's smoked turkey is herb butter or Cajun. Kelly's wears his signature: cherry Dr Pepper and brown sugar, the combination that crackles the bark on his ribs and chicken, here as a spritz and a reduced glaze over cherry wood. He injects his turkeys, always — chicken broth and butter, shot in warm. The skin comes off the smoker deep red mahogany and crackling, and there is not another bird like it on any Thanksgiving table.

items: 1 batch Ember Cherry Dr Pepper Spritz

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Stir the salt and sugar into the water till melted, sink the turkey in, and refrigerate overnight. (This is the Smoke & Ember Turkey Brine — it is what keeps a long smoke juicy.)

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Whisk the melted butter into the warm chicken broth and cherry Dr Pepper with the Worcestershire, garlic powder, and rub. Inject it warm — all over the breast, down into the thighs and legs. Butter sets cold, so warm is not a suggestion.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the skin dry and season with the salt, pepper, and garlic. Keep it simple — the glaze is the star of this bird.

steps.title: Smoke and spritz
steps.body: 275°F over cherry wood. Leave it alone the first 90 minutes so the skin sets, then spritz with the Cherry Dr Pepper Spritz every 45 minutes or so.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Simmer the cherry Dr Pepper and brown sugar down to a syrup, stir in the butter, and brush it over the bird twice in the last 30–45 minutes, till the skin goes deep red mahogany and starts to crackle. Sugar darkens fast — stay close.

steps.title: Rest and carve
steps.body: Pull at 160°F in the breast (165°F in the thigh), tent, and rest 30 minutes before carving. Save the drippings — they make a gravy worth talking about.

proTips: Kelly injects his turkeys every time — poultry gets the chicken-broth butter injection, same as this one.
In a hurry? Spatchcock the bird flat — same brine, injection, and glaze, near half the time.
The glaze goes on late for a reason: sugar burns. Two coats at the end beats one early coat every time.

title: Will's Onion Bombs
summary: Ground venison and pork — the pork brings the fat the deer can't — stuffed into sweet onion shells with a cheese center, wrapped in bacon, smoked, and glazed heavy with Ember sauce.
story: An onion bomb is a meatloaf wearing an onion for a jacket and bacon for a coat. Kelly's version runs on deer burger and pork, half and half, because venison on its own is too lean to stay juicy — the pork does that job, and the finely diced pepper in the mix is his touch. Cheese hides in the middle. These come off the smoker looking like something you'd pay money for at a festival.

items: 4 oz cheddar or pepper jack, cut into cubes

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Venison, pork, rub, garlic, pepper, the diced bell pepper, breadcrumbs, and egg — mixed just till it holds together. The jalapeño goes in now too, if you want the heat.

steps.title: Build the shells
steps.body: Cut the onions in half across the middle, peel them, and separate the layers into cups. Match up the halves that fit together — those are your bombs.

steps.title: Fill and wrap
steps.body: Pack meat into an onion cup, press a cube of cheese into the center, cap it with more meat and the matching onion half. Wrap each bomb in 2 slices of bacon and toothpick it shut.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250–275°F over hickory or apple, about 2 to 2 1/2 hours, till the bacon is crisped and the center reads 160°F.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush Ember sauce all over for the last 20–30 minutes — and be generous. It should set shiny and drip a little.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest five minutes, pull the toothpicks, and cut one open at the table so everybody sees the cheese pull.

proTips: The 50/50 pork is not filler — venison is so lean it needs the fat, and the flavor stays deer.
Finely diced pepper is the key word. Big chunks push the shells apart; fine dice disappears into the mix.
Leftover bombs slice cold into the best sandwich you will eat all season.

title: Smoked Squirrel in Gravy
summary: Freddie Wash's squirrels — quartered, braised tender, and gravied the way he did them — with Kelly's hickory smoke added up front, Smoke & Ember style.
story: This one comes down from Freddie Wash, Kelly's ex-father-in-law, born 1920 in Midway, Kentucky, in the middle of horse country. Freddie grew up in the Depression and wasted nothing — and he taught Kelly a whole lot about deer hunting besides. Now, Freddie did not smoke his squirrels, and he did not chop them up: he quartered them, braised them slow till they were tender, and made the gravy. That braise and gravy are Freddie's, unchanged. The spell in the hickory smoke up front is Kelly's addition — his Smoke & Ember road to the same supper, same as his rabbit. Take grays over reds when you can: Freddie's table preferred the gray squirrels, the more tender of the two.

items: 2 gray squirrels, cleaned and cut into pieces

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Stir the salt and sugar into the water, sink the squirrel pieces in, and refrigerate 4 hours to overnight. Small game is lean — the brine keeps it from drying out in the smoke.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the pieces dry and dust with the salt, pepper, garlic powder, and paprika.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225°F over hickory or apple, 45 minutes to an hour, till the pieces take on good color.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Into a Dutch oven with the chicken broth and sliced onion, lid on, 300°F till the meat is falling off the bone — about an hour for a young squirrel, up to two for an old one. This is Freddie's step: quartered, braised tender, no shortcuts.

steps.title: Gravy
steps.body: Lift the pieces out. Melt the butter, whisk in the flour and cook it a minute, then whisk in the braising liquid and simmer till it coats a spoon. Salt and pepper to taste.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Squirrel back in its gravy, spooned over split biscuits or mashed potatoes.

proTips: Freddie preferred gray squirrels over reds — the grays are more tender. Reds eat fine; they just ask for the longer braise.
The braise-and-gravy heart of this is Freddie's; the smoke is Kelly's. His rabbit rides the same smoke-then-braise road.
Freddie wasted nothing, and squirrel makes the case: a couple of squirrels and a pan of biscuits is a full supper.

title: Freddie's Hickory Nut Pie
summary: Hickory nuts Freddie gathered, floated on a dark molasses filling — sweetened the old way, because Freddie's day didn't run on corn syrup.
story: Freddie Wash gathered hickory nuts — and black walnuts — the way a man of his time did everything: by hand, off the land, around Midway, Kentucky. This pie is built for those nuts. There is no corn syrup in it; back then there wasn't much of it to be had, and molasses did the sweetening, so molasses does it here — dark, deep, a little smoky all on its own. The nuts float up while it bakes and toast on top, same as a pecan pie, which stands to reason: hickory nuts look a whole lot like pecans. Cracking them is half the work, and Freddie would tell you that's exactly why the pie means something.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Whisk the eggs, molasses, brown sugar, melted butter, vanilla, and salt till smooth. Stir in the hickory nuts and pour it all into the crust — the nuts will find their way to the top on their own.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: 350°F for 45–55 minutes, till the edges are set and the center still has a little jiggle. If the crust browns too fast, tent it with foil.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool at least 2 hours before slicing — a molasses pie cuts clean when it's had its rest. Good plain; better with coffee.

proTips: Black walnuts swap in one-for-one — Freddie gathered both, and either one belongs in this pie.
No corn syrup on purpose. If your people want it tamer, half molasses and half syrup splits the difference, but the old way is all molasses.
Hickory nuts crack hard and pick slow. That labor is the price of the pie, and it's worth it.

title: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake
summary: Two spiced pumpkin bundts sandwiched into one great pumpkin — orange cream-cheese frosting and a sugar-cone stem. The Halloween centerpiece at Bub & Sissy's.
story: Kelly spotted this cake rolling through his feed and sent it straight over with orders: we definitely need this for Halloween. He's right. Two pumpkin spice bundts, trimmed level and sandwiched flat-to-flat, turn into one round pumpkin with the ridges already built in — the bundt pan does the carving for you. Orange cream-cheese frosting, a sugar cone for a stem, and it sits in the middle of the table like it grew there. Around this house, Halloween is not done halfway, and neither is this cake.

items: 2 cans (15 oz each) pumpkin purée — not pie filling
Chocolate frosting (or melted chocolate chips), for coating the cone

steps.title: Mix the batter — twice
steps.body: Don't double-mix in one giant bowl. Make the batter in two batches using half of everything each time: whisk the dry, whisk the pumpkin, oil, sugars, eggs, vanilla, and milk, then bring them together just till combined.

steps.title: Bake both bundts
steps.body: Grease and flour two bundt pans well — every ridge. 350°F for 50–60 minutes, till a toothpick comes out clean. Rest 15 minutes in the pan, turn out, and cool completely. Warm cake and frosting are enemies.

steps.title: Stack the pumpkin
steps.body: Trim the flat side of each cake level with a serrated knife. Spread frosting on one flat side, set the second cake on it flat-to-flat — bottom dome down, top dome up — and line the ridges up so they run continuous. There's your pumpkin.

steps.title: Frost it orange
steps.body: Beat the frosting, tint it with gel coloring a shade deeper than you want — it lightens as it sits. Thin crumb coat first, chill 20 minutes, then the final coat, following the ridges.

steps.title: Stem and serve
steps.body: Coat the sugar cone in chocolate frosting, let it set a few minutes, and press it into the center hole on top. Slice with a serrated knife and watch the table go quiet.

proTips: Gel coloring, never the liquid drops — liquid thins the frosting and it slides off the ridges.
In a pinch, a mini peanut butter cup makes a fine stem too.
Like most spice cakes, this one's better on day two. Bake it the day before the party and frost it the morning of.

title: Smoked Candied Sweet Potatoes
summary: The old Southern candied sweet potatoes, smoked in two rounds — the glaze finishes uncovered in the smoke, with toasted pecans over the top.
story: Everybody knows the candied sweet potatoes off the holiday table — sliced in a pan, drowned in butter and brown sugar till they shine. This is that dish, moved outside. The potatoes smoke whole first, then get sliced and shingled in cast iron with the sugar and butter, and the pan goes back on the smoker uncovered — so the glaze thickens in the smoke instead of under a lid, and every slice comes out lacquered. Kelly's finishing touch: toasted pecans scattered over the top, because soft and sweet wants a little crunch.

items: 1 tsp vanilla — added at the end

steps.title: Smoke them whole
steps.body: Sweet potatoes right on the grate over pecan at 250–275°F, about 1 1/2 hours, till they just give when you squeeze them. Sweet wood for a sweet dish.

steps.title: Slice and shingle
steps.body: Cool till you can handle them, peel, and cut into 1/2-inch rounds. Shingle the rounds in a cast-iron skillet, dot the butter over, mix the sugars, cinnamon, nutmeg, and salt and rain it on, then pour the orange juice over all.

steps.title: Back on the smoker, uncovered
steps.body: 30–45 more minutes till the sugar melts into a syrup and bubbles at the edges. Leave the pan uncovered — that's the whole point. The glaze thickens and drinks the smoke at the same time.

steps.title: Vanilla and pecans
steps.body: Off the heat, stir the vanilla through — vanilla cooked hard just disappears; at the end it sings. Scatter the toasted pecans over the top and take the whole skillet to the table.

proTips: Turbinado sugar in place of the white gives the tops that crackle — use it if you've got it.
Toast the pecans in a dry skillet 3–4 minutes till they smell like they mean it, or in a small pan right on the smoker while the potatoes finish.
Leftovers reheat mean in a skillet for breakfast, next to eggs.

title: Broccoli Salad
summary: The sweet-tangy potluck broccoli salad — cheddar, bacon, sunflower seeds, craisins, and cherry tomatoes in a creamy dressing.
story: No barbecue table is complete without it: raw broccoli in a sweet-tangy dressing with cheddar, bacon, and crunch. A lot of folks make it with raisins — Kelly and Kristy use craisins, and once you've had it their way the dried cranberries just belong there, tart little pops against the bacon and cheese. Make it ahead; it gets better while it chills.

items: 2 heads broccoli, cut small — about 6 cups florets
6 slices bacon, cooked crisp and crumbled
Salt and black pepper to taste

steps.title: Cut the broccoli small
steps.body: Bite-size florets, small enough to eat off a fork with everything else. Big chunks make a salad nobody can get a full bite of.

steps.title: Whisk the dressing
steps.body: Mayo, vinegar, sugar, salt, and pepper till smooth. It should taste sweet first, tangy second.

steps.title: Toss it together
steps.body: Broccoli, onion, cheddar, bacon, craisins, and the cherry tomatoes in a big bowl; dressing over; fold till everything's coated and creamy.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Into the fridge at least an hour — overnight is better, the broccoli drinks the dressing in. Scatter the sunflower seeds over at serving so they stay crunchy.

proTips: Your own smoked bacon, crumbled, takes this clear over the top.
Cutting the broccoli small is the whole secret — it eats like a salad, not a chore.

title: Classic Creamy Coleslaw
summary: The classic creamy slaw — finely shredded cabbage in a sweet-tangy mayo dressing. The one that goes on the pulled pork sandwich.
story: Every barbecue joint has a slaw, and this is the classic the others get measured by: cabbage cut fine, a creamy dressing that's sweet first and tangy second, and an hour in the fridge to let it settle. It belongs beside the beans, on top of a pulled pork sandwich, and anywhere a plate needs something cool and crunchy to cut the smoke.

items: 1 head green cabbage, finely shredded — about 8 cups
1/4 small head purple cabbage, finely shredded (for color)

steps.title: Shred it fine
steps.body: Cabbage cut thin — fine shreds carry the dressing better and eat softer. Knife or the shredding disc, just keep it thin.

steps.title: Whisk the dressing
steps.body: Mayo, vinegar, sugar, celery seed, salt, and pepper till smooth. Taste it plain: sweet up front, a little bite behind.

steps.title: Toss and rest
steps.body: Dressing over the cabbage and carrot; toss till every shred's coated. Into the fridge at least an hour — the cabbage softens a touch and the flavors marry.

steps.title: Serve it cold
steps.body: One more toss before it goes out. Beside the plate or right on the sandwich — both are correct.

proTips: Dress it about an hour ahead, no earlier — slaw dressed the night before goes soupy.
Leftover slaw on a fried bologna sandwich the next day is not a compromise. It's a plan.

title: Cold-Smoked Cream Cheese
summary: Kelly's way: a cream cheese block cold-smoked under 90°F so it stays firm and sliceable, rested overnight, pepper jelly over the top.
story: Most folks hot-smoke their cream cheese till it's soft. Kelly cold-smokes his — the block never gets hot, so it takes on deep smoke flavor and stays firm enough to slice, like a smoked cheese should. The patience is in the rest: wrapped overnight in the fridge, the smoke mellows from harsh to smooth. Slice it for crackers, crumble it into eggs, or just stand at the counter with a knife. Nobody's judging.

items: 1 tsp olive oil or yellow mustard, for a binder
1–2 Tbsp Ember Sweet Heat Rub (or your favorite rub)
Pepper jelly, spooned over the top

steps.title: Score and rub
steps.body: Cold block on foil. Crosshatch the top about 1/4 inch deep, light coat of binder, then rub all over — tops and sides — so the smoke has something to grab.

steps.title: Cold smoke it
steps.body: Into smoke under 90°F — a smoke tube, a cold-smoke generator, or the faintest fire you can keep. The block should never get warm. 2–3 hours, apple wood if you've got it: mild and a little sweet.

steps.title: Rest it overnight
steps.body: Wrap the block tight and into the fridge overnight, a full day if you can stand it. Cold-smoked cheese tastes harsh right off the smoke; the rest is where it turns smooth.

steps.title: Slice and serve
steps.body: Pepper jelly spooned over the top, crackers around. It slices clean — or let it warm on the counter a bit if you want it spreadable after all.

proTips: Cold day? Even better — cold smoking is winter work, and the block stays firm without a fight.
A pan of ice in the smoker helps hold the temperature down on a warm day.

title: Smoked Cream Cheese (Hot & Soft)
summary: The other road: a cream cheese block smoked at 225°F till it's soft, puffed, and spreadable, with pepper jelly over the top.
story: Same little block, opposite treatment. At 225°F the cream cheese doesn't melt into a puddle — the stabilizers in it hold the shape — but it goes soft all the way through, puffs a little, and turns into the best warm dip nobody had to stir. Set it out with the pepper jelly running down and a pile of crackers, and watch it vanish. Kelly cold-smokes his (that recipe's here too); this is the hot road, and there's no wrong answer.

items: 1 tsp olive oil or yellow mustard, for a binder
1–2 Tbsp Ember Sweet Heat Rub (or your favorite rub)
Pepper jelly, warmed and spooned over

steps.title: Score and rub
steps.body: Cold block on foil — cold holds the shape better going in. Crosshatch the top 1/4 inch deep, light binder, rub all over.

steps.title: Smoke it low and slow
steps.body: 225°F, about 2 hours, apple or cherry wood. It'll soften, puff slightly, and go golden on top. Don't run it hotter or longer — past that it starts to weep and spread.

steps.title: Jelly and serve warm
steps.body: Spoon warm pepper jelly over the top and take it straight to the people, crackers alongside. Serve it warm, while it's still spreadable-soft.

proTips: Hot honey in place of the pepper jelly for the sweet-heat crowd — or pickled jalapeños over the top for the ones who want a kick.
Leftovers (there won't be) fold into scrambled eggs like they were born there.

title: Southern Sweet Tea
summary: The house wine of the South — five Luzianne bags to the gallon, a pinch of baking soda to keep it clear, poured over a glass packed with ice.
story: There's no barbecue plate in the South that doesn't come with a glass of this beside it. Kelly brews his strong — five family-size Luzianne bags to the gallon, steeped a full 15 minutes — because weak tea over melting ice is just brown water by the second refill. The pinch of baking soda is the old-timers' secret: it keeps the tea pouring clear and smooth instead of cloudy and sharp. Make a gallon. It won't last the weekend.

items: Cold water, to fill to 1 gallon

steps.title: Boil and sweeten
steps.body: Bring the 4 cups of water to a boil and take it off the heat. Stir in the baking soda and the sugar till the sugar melts clean.

steps.title: Steep 15 minutes
steps.body: Tea bags in for a full 15 minutes — off the boil, never boiling with the bags in, that's where bitter comes from. Lift the bags out and let them drain; don't wring them hard.

steps.title: Fill and chill
steps.body: Pour the tea into a gallon pitcher, top with cold water to the gallon mark, stir, and into the fridge till it's good and cold.

steps.title: Serve it right
steps.body: Over a glass packed full of ice — half-measures on the ice is how good tea goes watery. Lemon wedge if somebody's fancy.

proTips: Half tea, half lemonade over ice is the famous half-and-half — worth it on the hottest day of the year.
Keeps 3–4 days in the fridge, but it has never once lasted that long.

title: Real Lemonade
summary: Real lemonade — fresh lemons, sugar, water, and a pinch of salt. Nothing from a powder, ever.
story: Lemonade the way it was made before the powder mixes showed up: lemons squeezed by hand, sugar melted into hot water so it disappears clean, and a pinch of salt that you can't taste but that makes the lemon taste more like itself. This is the glass that sits next to the sweet tea at every cookout, and half-and-half with that tea — that's the third drink hiding inside these two.

items: 1 1/2 cups fresh lemon juice — 8 to 10 lemons
Ice and lemon slices, for serving

steps.title: Melt the sugar
steps.body: Sugar into the hot water, stir till it's clear as glass. Lemonade made with undissolved sugar is gritty at the bottom and sour at the top.

steps.title: Squeeze the lemons
steps.body: Roll each lemon hard on the counter first — it gives up more juice. Squeeze to 1 1/2 cups; strain out the seeds, keep a little pulp if you like it honest.

steps.title: Stir it together
steps.body: Syrup, lemon juice, cold water, and the pinch of salt in a pitcher. Chill it cold.

steps.title: Serve over ice
steps.body: Full glass of ice, lemon slice on the rim if you're showing off.

proTips: Too tart? A tablespoon of sugar at a time — lemonade should bite a little, that's its job.

title: Peach Sweet Tea
summary: Kelly's sweet tea — five Luzianne bags, 15-minute steep — with ripe peaches simmered into the sugar first.
story: Start with Kelly's sweet tea exactly the way he makes it — five family-size Luzianne bags, a 15-minute steep — and run ripe summer peaches through the sugar water before the tea ever touches it. The peaches simmer, get mashed, and give the whole gallon a round, honeyed fruit flavor underneath the tea. August in a glass, and it was made for a plate of ribs.

items: Cold water, to fill to 1 gallon
Ice and peach slices, for serving

steps.title: Simmer the peaches
steps.body: Peaches, sugar, and the 4 cups of water in a pot; simmer 15 minutes, mashing the peaches soft with a spoon as they go.

steps.title: Steep the tea in it
steps.body: Off the heat. Baking soda in, then the tea bags — steep 15 minutes, Kelly's timing. Bags out, drain, don't wring.

steps.title: Strain and fill
steps.body: Pour through a strainer into the gallon pitcher, pressing the peaches for every drop. Cold water to the gallon mark.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Fridge till cold, over a full glass of ice, peach slice on the rim.

proTips: Frozen peaches work when fresh ones aren't in season — the tea doesn't mind.

title: Watermelon Lemonade
summary: Half a watermelon blended and strained, sharpened with lemon — pink, ice-cold, and gone by supper.
story: Every summer there's a watermelon too big to finish, and this is its second life. Blended and strained, sweetened just a touch, and cut with lemon juice so it drinks bright instead of flat-sweet. It pours the color of a sunset and the kids treat the pitcher like it owes them money.

items: About 8 cups watermelon chunks, seeds out — half a medium melon
3/4 cup fresh lemon juice — 5 to 6 lemons
Ice and watermelon wedges, for serving

steps.title: Blend the melon
steps.body: Watermelon chunks in the blender till it's juice. Strain through a sieve, pressing the pulp — you want it smooth, not slushy.

steps.title: Cut it with lemon
steps.body: Lemon juice, sugar, salt, and the cold water stirred in. Taste: it should be watermelon first, lemonade right behind it.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Cold as you can get it, over ice, little watermelon wedge on the rim.

proTips: Make it the same day you serve it — watermelon juice is best fresh and knows it.

title: Sherbet Punch
summary: The church-potluck crown: ginger ale over rainbow sherbet with pineapple juice, foaming in the big bowl.
story: Every church supper, baby shower, and family reunion in the South has this bowl in the middle of the table: rainbow sherbet melting into ginger ale, foaming up pastel, sweet enough to make the kids orbit it like a porch light. Five minutes to make, and Bub and Sissy will drain it to the ladle. Some things don't need improving — they need refilling.

items: 1 (2-liter) bottle lemon-lime soda, cold (optional, for extra fizz)

steps.title: Build the bowl
steps.body: Pineapple juice in the punch bowl first, then the sherbet in big scoops all over the top.

steps.title: Pour the fizz
steps.body: Ginger ale (and the lemon-lime, if you're using it) poured slow over the sherbet so it foams up proud instead of fizzing out.

steps.title: Ladle it out
steps.body: Serve right away, a little sherbet in every cup. Refill as needed — it will be needed.

proTips: Everything cold before you start, including the bowl if you can manage it — warm punch goes flat and sad.
Adults doctoring their own cup at their own end is between them and the cup.

title: Blackberry Sweet Tea
summary: Kelly's sweet tea — five Luzianne bags, 15-minute steep — with wild-style blackberries simmered into the sugar. Deep purple and fence-row sweet.
story: Blackberries grow wild along every fence row and creek bank in Kentucky, free for the picking if you mind the thorns and the snakes. Freddie Wash taught Kelly about dewberries, the blackberry's wild little trailing cousin, and any Kentucky kid who picked berries till his fingers stained purple knows what this tea is about. It's Kelly's sweet tea — five Luzianne bags, a 15-minute steep — with the berries simmered into the sugar first, so the whole gallon pours the color of a blackberry patch at dusk.

items: Cold water, to fill to 1 gallon
Ice and fresh blackberries, for serving

steps.title: Simmer the berries
steps.body: Blackberries, sugar, and the 4 cups of water; simmer about 15 minutes, mashing the berries well — you want every drop of that purple out of them.

steps.title: Steep the tea in it
steps.body: Off the heat, baking soda in, then the bags for 15 minutes. Out, drained, not wrung.

steps.title: Strain it clean
steps.body: Through a fine strainer into the gallon pitcher — blackberries carry seeds, and nobody wants them in a glass of tea. Press the pulp, then cold water to the gallon mark.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Cold, over a full glass of ice, a few fresh berries dropped in the glass.

proTips: Frozen blackberries work fine out of season — wild ones in July are better and you know it.

title: Raspberry Sweet Tea
summary: Kelly's sweet tea with raspberries in the syrup — brighter and tarter than the peach, ruby red in the glass.
story: Same Luzianne spine as all of Kelly's teas — five bags, 15 minutes — but raspberries bring a brightness the other fruits don't. They run tart, so the tea pours ruby red and lively, sweet up front with a little zing behind it. The one to make when the ribs are rich and the day is hot.

items: Cold water, to fill to 1 gallon
Ice and fresh raspberries, for serving

steps.title: Simmer the berries
steps.body: Raspberries, sugar, and the 4 cups of water; simmer about 10 minutes, mashing as they soften and fall apart.

steps.title: Steep the tea in it
steps.body: Off the heat, soda in, bags in for 15 minutes. Out and drained.

steps.title: Strain and fill
steps.body: Strain into the gallon pitcher — raspberry seeds are small and sneaky — press the pulp, cold water to the mark.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Over a full glass of ice with a few fresh raspberries riding on top.

proTips: Raspberries run tart — if your batch bites too hard, stir in sugar a spoonful at a time while it's still warm.

title: Chicken Bacon Ranch Pizza

items: 1 lb pizza dough ball, at room temperature 30 minutes
1/2 cup ranch dressing, plus more for the drizzle
2 cups chopped smoked chicken (leftover is perfect; thighs stay juiciest)
8 slices bacon, cooked crisp and crumbled
1 (14.5 oz) can fire-roasted diced tomatoes, drained well
1 clove garlic, minced (or 1/4 tsp garlic powder)

steps.title: Heat the stone
steps.body: Set a pizza stone or steel on the grill or smoker grates, lid down, and run it as hot as it'll go — 550°F or better — for a full 30 to 45 minutes. That stored heat is the whole brick-oven trick.

steps.title: Stretch the dough
steps.body: On a cornmeal-dusted surface, stretch the dough to 12 to 14 inches, leaving a fat rim around the edge for the crust.

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: Spread the ranch thin inside the rim as the sauce. Mozzarella first, then the chicken, bacon crumbles, red onion, and the drained tomatoes. Monterey Jack and parmesan go over the top of everything.

steps.title: Launch and bake
steps.body: Slide the pizza onto the hot stone, lid down, 6 to 9 minutes, turning once, until the crust is blistered and spotted and the cheese bubbles with brown freckles.

steps.title: Rest and finish
steps.body: Off the heat, rest 2 to 3 minutes — pizza needs a rest like anything else. Brush the rim with the garlic butter, zigzag a drizzle of ranch over the top, scatter the green onions, then slice and serve.

summary: Kristy's chicken bacon ranch pizza: smoked chicken, crumbled bacon, and red onion over ranch with mozzarella and Monterey Jack, stone-fired and brushed with garlic butter.
story: The first pizza ever on Smoke and Ember comes from Kristy's side of the kitchen: smoked chicken and a heavy hand of crumbled bacon over a ranch base — no red sauce — with red onion and fire-roasted tomatoes, mozzarella under a melted Monterey Jack blanket, and a garlic-butter crust.
proTips: Wet tomatoes make a soggy middle — drain them, then blot with a paper towel if they're stubborn.
No stone? A cast iron skillet flipped upside down on the grate does the same job.
Cold leftover smoked chicken is the move here; this pizza was born for leftovers.

title: Oatmeal Cookies with White Chocolate & Craisins

steps.title: Cream it
steps.body: Beat the butter and both sugars until fluffy, about 2 minutes. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.

steps.title: Dry in
steps.body: Stir the flour, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt together, then mix into the butter just until it's in.

steps.title: Oats and the good stuff
steps.body: Fold in the oats, then the white chocolate chips and Craisins, until every scoop's got some of everything.

steps.title: Scoop and bake
steps.body: Rounded tablespoons of dough, 2 inches apart on a parchment-lined sheet. Bake at 350°F for 10 to 12 minutes, until the edges are golden and the centers still look a touch soft.

steps.title: Rest on the pan
steps.body: Five minutes on the hot pan before moving them — they finish setting up there, and that's the difference between chewy and crumbly.

summary: Chewy oatmeal cookies loaded with white chocolate chips and Craisins — never raisins — soft in the middle with crisp edges.
story: Chewy oatmeal cookies loaded with creamy white chocolate chips and tart little bursts of cranberry. Same rule as the broccoli salad around this house: it's Craisins, never raisins — and in a cookie, that sweet-tart pop against the white chocolate is exactly right.
proTips: Pull them when the centers look slightly underdone — carryover heat finishes them and keeps the chew.
A pinch of orange zest in the dough plays real nice with the cranberry, if you're feeling fancy.
Dough freezes in scoops; bake from frozen with 2 extra minutes.

items: 2 lbs red potatoes, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch chunks (Yukon Golds work too)
1 1/2 lbs smoked sausage or kielbasa, sliced into 1/2-inch coins
The bacon drippings are the base — nothing extra needed

steps.body: Peeled chunks in salted water, 10 to 12 minutes, until a knife slides in easy. Scoop out 1/4 cup of the cooking water, then drain — and keep the potatoes warm.
steps.title: Boil the potatoes

steps.body: In a big cast iron skillet over medium-high, brown the sausage coins on both sides. Lift them out; leave the grease in the pan.
steps.title: Sear the sausage

steps.body: Bacon in the same skillet until crisp; lift it out. Onion into the drippings, 3 to 4 minutes, until soft.
steps.title: Bacon and onion

steps.body: Kill the heat. Whisk the vinegar, sugar, mustard, salt, pepper, and the hot potato water right into the drippings and onions, scraping up the browned bits. It'll sizzle and smell sharp — that's right.
steps.title: Make the dressing in the pan

steps.body: Potatoes, sausage, and bacon back in; fold gentle until everything's glossy with dressing. The warm potatoes drink it up as they sit.
steps.title: Toss it warm

steps.body: Cast iron onto the smoker at 250°F for 20 minutes to warm through and catch a little smoke. Sprinkle the cheddar over the top for the last 5 minutes so it melts in. Green onions over everything — serve warm right out of the pan.
steps.title: Smoke finish

title: Hot German Potato Salad with Smoked Sausage
summary: Warm German potato salad with smoked sausage coins in a bacon-vinegar dressing, cheddar melted over the top, finished on the smoker in cast iron.
story: No mayo anywhere near it — the old German way: tender potatoes and seared smoked sausage tossed warm in a bacon-vinegar dressing, then warmed through on the smoker in cast iron. Kelly's way runs sausage-heavy, the bacon crumbled fine and plenty of it, shredded cheddar melting over the top, and green onions to finish.
proTips: Dress the potatoes warm, never cold — cold potatoes shed dressing, warm ones drink it in.
Too sharp? A second teaspoon of sugar rounds the vinegar without making it sweet.
It reheats beautifully; splash a spoonful of vinegar over leftovers to wake it back up.

title: Kristy's Potato Soup

items: 3 lbs potatoes, peeled and cut into a 3/4-inch dice
Water and chicken stock, to cover (about 4 cups stock)
1 lb shredded cheddar, plus more for serving
1 bunch green onions, diced — some for the soup, some for serving
Salt and black pepper, to taste
About 4 cups milk, divided — more as needed for the thickness you want

steps.title: Boil the potatoes
steps.body: Cut potatoes in a pot, cover with water and chicken stock, and boil until just tender.

steps.title: Fry the bacon
steps.body: While the potatoes cook, fry the bacon in a skillet. Crumble it and set it aside — and save the bacon grease for your roux.

steps.title: Onions in the grease
steps.body: When the potatoes are just tender, sauté the diced onion in the bacon grease until tender.

steps.title: Make the roux
steps.body: Stir the flour into the onion and bacon grease, then add milk a little at a time, stirring until smooth.

steps.title: Thicken the pot
steps.body: With the potatoes still boiling, stir the roux into the pot. Pour in more milk until the soup hits the thickness you want. Keep stirring.

steps.title: Load it
steps.body: Add the diced ham, diced green onions, the pound of shredded cheese, the cup of sour cream, salt and pepper — then stir the crumbled bacon in. Stir everything together until the cheese melts through.

steps.title: Serve it
steps.body: Ladle it up, then sprinkle cheese and green onion over the top of every bowl — spread out, not piled.

summary: Kristy's loaded potato soup: bacon-grease roux, diced ham, a pound of cheddar, sour cream, and crumbled bacon — cheese and green onion over every bowl.
story: Kristy's potato soup: potatoes boiled in chicken stock, thickened with a bacon-grease roux, then loaded with diced ham, green onions, a full pound of shredded cheese, a cup of sour cream, and the crumbled bacon stirred in. Every bowl finished with cheese and green onion spread over the top.
proTips: Stir steady once the roux goes in — a roux-thickened soup will scorch if it sits still.
Even better the next day; thin it with a splash of milk when you reheat.

title: Smoked Turducken
summary: Three birds in one: a chicken inside a duck inside a turkey, a different dressing inside every bird, smoked low over oak and pecan until the very center reads 165°.
story: Three birds, boned and nested — a chicken rolled inside a duck, the duck rolled inside a turkey, a different dressing inside every bird — sewn up, trussed, and smoked low until the very middle is done. It landed on the app by request, ahead of the holidays: the biggest showpiece in American cooking, done the Smoke-Ember way.
