Kelly hasn't cooked one yet — this build follows the best-rated classic, smoked instead of roasted — and the day he does, his verdict goes right here.

items: 1 whole turkey, 20-25 lbs, deboned except wing tips and drumstick bones
Smoke & Ember Turkey Brine, enough for all three birds (optional, overnight)
Creole seasoning, salt, and black pepper
1 cup of the savory bread stuffing

steps.title: Brine overnight
steps.body: All three birds in the brine, fridge, 12 to 24 hours. Out, rinsed, patted dry — and kept COLD from here on.

steps.title: Make the three dressings
steps.body: Mix all three dressings and chill them. Cold dressing and cold birds is the rule for the whole build.

steps.title: Debone the birds (or don't)
steps.body: Deboning all three is the hardest hour of the recipe; a good butcher will do it if you ask a few days ahead. The turkey keeps its wing tips and drumstick bones so it still looks like a turkey; the duck and chicken come fully boneless.

steps.title: Butter and season
steps.body: Herb butter worked under the turkey's skin from the outside; every bird's meat side seasoned well with Creole seasoning, salt, and pepper.

steps.title: Stuff the chicken
steps.body: Chicken flat, skin-side down. Cornbread dressing spread over it; roll the chicken up around the dressing and skewer it shut — a plump little stuffed chicken.

steps.title: Stuff the duck
steps.body: Duck flat, skin-side down, cranberry-pecan dressing spread over it. The stuffed chicken goes in the middle; fold the duck around it and skewer it shut.

steps.title: Stuff the turkey
steps.body: Turkey flat, skin-side down, savory bread stuffing spread over it, and the whole duck bundle in the middle. Cheap insurance: inject the turkey breast with warm butter-broth before you close it. With a helper, fold the turkey up, sew the back seam (or skewer and lace it), truss it firm, and set it breast-up in a big roasting pan on a rack, legs tied to look proper.

steps.title: Smoke it
steps.body: 250-275°F over oak or pecan, pan and all, until a probe pushed to the very center reads 165°F — plan on 8 to 9 hours. Drain drippings every couple of hours (they'll make a gallon of gravy), and tent with foil if the skin gets ahead of the middle.

steps.title: Rest it a full hour
steps.body: No bones means no frame; the rest is what lets it slice clean. Move it with two big spatulas underneath, never by the legs.

steps.title: Carve across
steps.body: Slice crosswise so every slice carries all three birds and all three dressings. Serve with the extra dressings — baked at 350°F while the bird rested — and gravy from the drippings.

proTips: The 165° reading must come from the dead center — the middle of the chicken. Check it in two spots before you call it done.
Everything stays cold during assembly. Work steady, and if the build runs long, get it back in the fridge for a spell.
Ask the butcher a few days ahead — holiday week is not the time to surprise him with three birds to bone.
Leftover slices fry up in a skillet like the best deli meat you ever had.

title: Smoked Baked Sweet Potatoes
summary: Whole sweet potatoes smoked till they squeeze soft, split and fluffed with cinnamon butter, crowned with toasted marshmallows and a warm caramel drizzle.
story: The baked potato's sweeter Southern cousin, cooked the lazy right way: the potatoes ride the smoker alongside whatever meat is on, and by the time the meat rests, dessert's half done. Cinnamon butter in the split, marshmallows toasted right on top, caramel over it all — a side dish that eats like the end of the meal.

items: 4 large sweet potatoes, scrubbed and dried
1 Tbsp oil or melted butter, for the skins

steps.title: Rub and salt
steps.body: Scrub the potatoes, dry them well, rub the skins with oil, and salt them all over. The salted skin is half the flavor.

steps.title: Smoke them
steps.body: 250-275°F over pecan or oak, right alongside whatever meat is cooking. Two to two and a half hours, until they give when you squeeze them and a knife slides in with no fight at all. They're done by feel, not by the clock.

steps.title: Split and butter
steps.body: Split each potato lengthwise, fluff the insides with a fork, and drop a big spoonful of cinnamon butter into each one while they're steaming.

steps.title: Toast the marshmallows
steps.body: Scatter the mini marshmallows over the tops and give them 3 to 5 more minutes of heat until they're puffed and golden. Watch them close — marshmallows go from golden to gone in a hurry.

steps.title: Caramel and serve
steps.body: Drizzle the warm caramel over the tops and serve right away, while the marshmallows are still soft.

proTips: Pick potatoes all about the same size so they finish together.
Set them on when the meat goes on — they ask nothing and keep it company the whole cook.
Leftover smoked sweet potatoes mash into the best casserole base you ever started with.

title: Smoked Sweet Potato Casserole
summary: Smoked sweet potatoes mashed with brown sugar, butter, and cinnamon under a pecan crunch — with toasted marshmallows on top, because this house does both.
story: The Thanksgiving pan, Smoke-Ember style: it starts with smoked sweet potatoes, so the filling carries a whisper of smoke under all that brown sugar. Some houses fight over pecan crunch versus marshmallows on top. Not this one — here it gets both, and the argument is over before it starts.

steps.title: Cook the potatoes
steps.body: Smoke at 250-275°F until they squeeze soft, about 2 hours — same as the Smoked Baked Sweet Potatoes — or bake at 400°F for about an hour. Scoop out the flesh and leave the skins behind.

steps.title: Mash the filling
steps.body: Mash the flesh with the brown sugar, melted butter, milk, eggs, vanilla, cinnamon, and salt until smooth.

steps.title: Into the skillet
steps.body: Spread the filling in a buttered cast iron skillet or baking dish and smooth the top.

steps.title: The pecan crunch
steps.body: Cut the cold butter into the brown sugar, flour, and pecans until crumbly, and scatter it evenly over the whole top.

steps.title: Smoke it
steps.body: 325-350°F for 25 to 30 minutes, until the crunch is crisp and the edges are bubbling.

steps.title: Marshmallows last
steps.body: Scatter the mini marshmallows over the top and give it 5 more minutes, until they're puffed and toasted. Serve it hot.

proTips: Start with smoked potatoes if you can — the filling carries a whisper of smoke no oven can fake.
Marshmallows go on last and get watched: golden in minutes, gone not long after.
It reheats fine, but put fresh marshmallows on for the reheat so the top looks alive.

title: Ember Navy Beans and Ham
finish: Beans tender throughout; broth coats a spoon
summary: Navy beans, country ham, and a thick broth with no flour and no cream — mash some of the beans right in the pot and let them do the thickening.
story: This is my take on the old Southern pot of beans and ham. The ham is country ham, browned right in the pot you are going to cook in, and you save the grease that comes off it and cook the onion in that grease. No bay leaves, no garlic powder, no onion powder, and no bacon drippings unless you happen to have them. The beans simmer low until they are tender all the way through, then you mash a cup of them back into the pot and let the beans thicken their own broth. Salt last and taste first, because the ham is salty enough to season the whole pot. Serve it hot with a wedge of cast-iron cornbread for sopping.

items: 1 lb dried navy beans, picked over and rinsed
1 lb country ham pieces, or a smoked ham hock, or leftover smoked ham, diced
8 cups water, or chicken broth if you have it
Salt only at the end — the ham brings plenty

steps.body: Cover the navy beans with water by a couple inches and soak overnight. Drain and rinse before cooking.
steps.title: Soak overnight

steps.body: Brown the diced country ham in the pot you are going to cook in — if you have bacon grease on hand, brown it in that instead. Set the ham aside and save the grease that came off it, then cook the onion in that grease until softened and stir in the garlic for 30 seconds. A ham hock goes straight in the pot, no browning needed.
steps.title: Brown the ham, save the grease

steps.body: Add the drained beans, the ham, the onion and garlic, and the water or broth. No bay leaves, no garlic powder, no onion powder, no bacon drippings in this pot.
steps.title: Build the pot

steps.body: Bring it up to a gentle boil, then cut it back to a simmer, lid cracked. Let it go 2–3 hours, stirring now and then, until the beans are tender all the way through.
steps.title: Simmer low

steps.body: Fish out the hock, pull the meat off the bone, chop it, and stir it back in. Toss the bone.
steps.title: Pull the meat

steps.body: Scoop out about a cup of beans, mash them against the side of the pot with a spoon, and stir them back in. No flour, no cream — the beans thicken their own broth. Let it simmer another 15 minutes until it coats a spoon.
steps.title: Thicken it the old way

steps.body: Pepper to taste, then salt only if it needs it. Taste first — the ham is salty.
steps.title: Season last

steps.body: Ladle it up hot with a wedge of cast-iron cornbread for sopping.
steps.title: Serve it hot

proTips.text: If the hock isn't smoked, smoke it first over hickory — real smoke from the smoker, never liquid smoke.
Leftovers are better the next day. Add a splash of water when you reheat — the broth keeps thickening as it sits.
Salt last and taste first. The ham is salty enough to season the whole pot.

proTips.text: No extra salt anywhere else in the cook — the bird's already brined and the rub carries the salt.
Poultry takes smoke fast — light hand on the wood.
Uncovered in the fridge is the point — it dries the skin so it crisps.

Spatchcock or leave it whole? Flat cooks faster and more even — the breast and legs finish closer together, and the skin crisps all over because nothing's tucked underneath. On a 12–14 lb bird at these temps, spatchcocking cuts about 1½–2 hours — roughly 4–5 hours whole, about 2½ hours flat. Same temps either way, just watch the thermometer closer on a flat bird, it moves faster.
